comments.author: Uttam Gupta
comments.comment: One term I’d add is “context window” - the amount of information a model can pay attention to at once. A lot of bad AI output is not because the model is weak, but because the right source, constraint, or example never made it into context.

comments.author: Justin C. Gohn, CRE®, MAI, SRA
comments.comment: The hard part is not letting the agent run longer, it is defining stop conditions it can actually verify. For research agents, I like forcing a coverage test: source diversity, duplicate rate, date bounds, and a final list of queries it tried but found nothing for. That last part is usually where you see whether it searched systematically or just got lucky.

comments.author: METTU MANOJ BABU
comments.comment: The most hireable fresher is usually the one who can show their debugging trail, not just the final project demo. A clean README with tradeoffs, failed attempts, eval results, and what you changed after feedback tells me more than a long certificate list. For AI roles, I’d add one more signal: can you measure whether the system got better after your prompt, retrieval, or model change?

comments.author: Reshma Sriraman
comments.comment: Credits help, but the real constraint is usually eval discipline. I’d spend the first week building a tiny regression suite around the 20-50 prompts that map to actual user pain, then use the free runway to test model, prompt, and tool changes against that baseline.

comments.author: Ronald M.
comments.comment:
The underrated part here is that “boring” strategies are easier to test, monitor, and kill when they drift.

A trading bot without backtests, position limits, failure handling, and clear stop conditions is just a fast way to automate bad decisions.

Sharp question: did you test it on periods where DCA looks terrible, like long drawdowns or sudden volatility spikes?
